It is in the file `methodpaper.pdf`\n    29→  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\n    30→- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `methods.txt`. \n    31→- **Code**:\n    32→  - `code` contains code from `methodpaper.pdf`.\n    33→- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `data`.\n    34→- **Documentation** on the NWB file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. \n    35→\n    36→## Decoder Task\n    37→\n    38→- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \n    39→- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\n    40→- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \n    41→\n    42→### Decoder Inputs:\n    43→- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\n    44→- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\n    45→\n    46→### Decoder Outputs\n    47→- Lick direction **choice** (left = 0, right = 1, per-trial)\n    48→- **Outcome** (ignore = 0, miss = 1, hit = 2, per-trial)\n    49→- **Early lick** (no = 0, yes = 1, per-trial)\n    50→- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\n    51→  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\n    52→  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n    53→  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\n    54→\n    55→## Target Data Format\n    56→\n    57→- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `converted_data.pkl`.\n    58→- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n    59→\n    60→```python\n    61→data = {\n    62→    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n    63→        [  # list of trials for session 1\n    64→            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n    65→            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n    66→            ...\n    67→        ],\n    68→        [  # list of trials for session 2\n    69→            ...\n    70→        ],\n    71→        ...\n    72→    ],\n    73→\n    74→    'input': [  # list of sessions\n    75→        [  # list of trials for session 1\n    76→            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n    77→            ...\n    78→        ],\n    79→        ...\n    80→    ],\n    81→\n    82→    'output': [  # list of sessions\n    83→        [  # list of trials for session 1\n    84→            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n    85→            ...\n    86→        ],\n    87→        ...\n    88→    ],\n    89→\n    90→    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\n    91→    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\n    92→\n    93→    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\n    94→    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\n    95→        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    96→    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n    97→\n    98→    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    99→    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n   100→    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n   101→        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n   102→        ...\n   103→    ],\n   104→\n   105→    'metadata': {\n   106→        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n   107→        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n   108→        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n   109→        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n   110→        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n   111→        ...\n   112→    }\n   113→}\n   114→```\n   115→\n   116→### Key Format Requirements\n   117→\n   118→- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n   119→  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n   120→  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n   121→  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n   122→\n   123→- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n   124→  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n   125→  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n   126→    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n   127→    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n   128→    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n   129→  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n   130→  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n   131→  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n   132→\n   133→- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n   134→  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n   135→  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n   136→  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n   137→  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n   138→  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n   139→\n   140→- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n   141→- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n   142→  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n   143→\n   144→- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n   145→- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n   146→\n   147→- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n   148→  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n   149→\n   150→- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n   151→  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n   152→- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n   153→  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n   154→\n   155→- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n   156→  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n   157→  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n   158→  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n   159→  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n   160→  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n   161→\n   162→## Python environment\n   163→\n   164→- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n   165→- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n   166→- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n   167→\n   168→## Decoder Reference\n   169→\n   170→- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n   171→- Optional arguments:\n   172→  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n   173→  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n   174→  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n   175→- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n   176→\n   177→### Purpose\n   178→\n   179→These functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n   180→1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n   181→2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n   182→3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \n   183→4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\n   184→5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\n   185→\n   186→### Consistency requirements\n   187→\n   188→Your processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\n   189→- Loading of data\n   190→- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\n   191→- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\n   192→- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\n   193→\n   194→To check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \n   195→\n   196→Whenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \n   197→\n   198→Discrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above. \n   199→\n   200→Carefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \n   201→\n   202→You will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \n   203→\n   204→---\n   205→\n   206→## Conversion Workflow\n   207→\n   208→**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. An index of '42' from this session means the 2nd (42-10-30) unit from p3.\n   162→            '''\n   163→            temp_list = list(glob.glob(os.path.join(qc_folder, '{}*.mat'.format(sess_name_qc))))\n   164→            assert len(temp_list) == 1\n   165→            filepath_qc = temp_list[0]\n   166→\n   167→            qc_file = preprocessing_utils.loadmat(filepath_qc)\n   168→            # idx_qc_dict = qc_file['Idx'] # dict. list of np.str_\n   202→        ccf_label = [str(x).strip() for x in ccf_label] # list of string, with both whitespace at the beginning and end of each string removed\n   203→\n   204→        # -- 1.2.4 get units that have both ephys and histology\n   205→        unit_comb = set(unit_info[:,0]) & set(ccf_unit_id) # HERE\n   328→            area_dict_exist = pickle.load(f)\n   329→            fr = area_dict_exist['fr']\n   330→            spike_times_area = area_dict_exist['spike_times']\n   331→            bin_centers = area_dict_exist['bin_centers']\n   332→\n   333→    # The reference code uses 40ms bin width with 3.4ms stride (sliding window), but the instructions explicitly specify 50ms bins.\n\n## 2-c. The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\n\nTwo CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). The cameras were equipped with 4-12 mm focal length lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron) and a pixel resolution of 71 mm. We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\n\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\n\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\n\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\n\nPhotoinhibition\n\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\n\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\n\nSpike sorting and quality control\n\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\n\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. Your goal is to load and reformat data from a neuroscience paper into a specified structure suitable for downstream analysis.\\n- You need to use the **SAME** processing of the data described in the provided reference paper and code repository. \\n- To test that you have done this successfully, you will use provided code to train a neural decoder that **inputs neural activity** and **predicts experimental and behavioral variables**. \\n- We will assess your correctness on **matching the loading and processing described in the reference texts and code**. \\n\\n## Reference Information\\n\\n- **Papers**:\\n  - Data were first presented in \\\"Brain-wide neural activity underlying memory-guided movement\\\". It is in the file `datapaper.pdf`\\n  - A recent paper that uses this dataset is \\\"Brain-wide analysis reveals movement encoding structured across and within brain areas\\\". It is in the file `methodpaper.pdf`\\n  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `methods.txt`. \\n- **Code**:\\n  - `code` contains code from `methodpaper.pdf`.\\n- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `data`.\\n- **Documentation** on the NWB file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. \\n\\n## Decoder Task\\n\\n- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \\n- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\\n- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \\n\\n### Decoder Inputs:\\n- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\\n- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\\n\\n### Decoder Outputs\\n- Lick direction **choice** (left = 0, right = 1, per-trial)\\n- **Outcome** (ignore = 0, miss = 1, hit = 2, per-trial)\\n- **Early lick** (no = 0, yes = 1, per-trial)\\n- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\\n  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\\n  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\\n  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\\n\\n## Target Data Format\\n\\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `converted_data.pkl`.\\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\\n\\n```python\\ndata = {\\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1.
